questions.question: Explain what a composite material is and the principle by which it is designed, and give three examples of composites used before the industrial age.
questions.expected_answer: A composite combines two or more materials, or layers of one material, so that the whole has properties no part has alone; the design principle is to place each component where the force it resists best will act. Pre-industrial examples: straw in mud bricks, where the straw fibres carry the tension that would otherwise crack the drying mud; laminated bows of wood, horn and sinew, with horn on the compressed belly and sinew on the stretched back; and wattle-and-daub walls, where woven sticks carry tension and bending inside the mud.

questions.question: Describe how plain concrete fails in bending, where reinforcing steel is placed in a simply supported beam and over a column, and the three properties that allow steel and concrete to work together.
questions.expected_answer: Plain concrete is strong in compression but about one tenth as strong in tension and brittle, so a bending beam cracks on its stretched underside and fails suddenly. In a simply supported beam the main bars run near the bottom, where the tension is, with concrete cover beneath them, while the concrete above the neutral axis carries compression; over a column the beam bends the other way so the bars are placed near the top; stirrups wrap the bars to resist shear and hold the cage. Cooperation depends on the ribbed bars gripping the concrete, steel and concrete expanding almost equally with temperature, and the alkaline concrete protecting the steel from rust when the cover is adequate.

questions.question: Explain how plywood is manufactured, which weaknesses of solid timber it overcomes, why the number of layers is odd, and what its own weaknesses are.
questions.expected_answer: Plywood is made by peeling a log into thin veneers and gluing an odd number of them with the grain of each layer at right angles to the one below. It overcomes timber's weakness across the grain, its tendency to split along the grain, and its warping and shrinking, because half the layers run in each direction, a split is stopped by crossed grain, and each layer restrains the movement of its neighbours; it also uses the log efficiently. The number is odd so that both face veneers run the same way and the sheet is balanced. Weaknesses: interior glue delaminates when wet, so exterior or marine grades are needed outdoors, and the edges split if screwed too close without drilling.
